artifacts.summary: Benchmarked literature-coverage-delta.sh against the live 11,545-entry global index: the per-entry jq triple-spawn is only ~30% of the cost; literature-term-match.sh's to_lower/term_matches subprocess forking is the dominant ~65-70%. Validated a combined fix (single-pass @tsv jq extraction + pure-bash term matching) at 181x speedup (33.36s -> 0.184s) with byte-identical candidate sets across 5 queries; recommends against caching and flags that literature-term-match.sh must be edited (relevant to the serialized FTS5 task's file-overlap gate).

memory_candidates.content: Bash helper functions that fork subprocesses per call (echo|tr, echo|grep) are frequently the dominant cost in a hot loop, not the more visible jq subprocess spawns around them. When profiling a bash script that loops over N items and calls a shared matching/normalization helper M times per item, benchmark the helper in isolation (e.g. 1000 bare calls) before assuming the per-item jq/external-tool calls are the bottleneck. Pure-bash replacements (${var,,} for lowercasing, [[ $a == *$b* ]] for substring match) eliminate the fork/exec cost entirely and are safe once bash 4+ is already an established baseline in the codebase.

jq's @tsv format-string escapes literal tab/newline/backslash characters within a field as two-character sequences rather than stripping or leaving them raw, so real tab separators between fields are never ambiguous when consumed by `while IFS=$'\t' read`. This makes @tsv safe as a field-delimiter format for jq-to-bash record extraction even when field content is untrusted, at the cost of a narrow cosmetic caveat: any field content containing those characters is exposed to the bash consumer in escaped form, not raw.
